messages.subject: size-biased sampling
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have a vector of animal speed measurements made from videos taken at random locations in the field. I’d like to uncover the pdf of animal speeds at the population level (and estimate mean animal speed). I strongly suspect that my measurements are a biased sample, since faster animals cover more ground and so are more likely to be observed.

In a likelihood framework, there is the potential to use size-biased distributions to account for the fact that faster speeds are over-represented in the dataset, but I’m currently at a loss as to how these ideas might be applied in a hierarchical modelling framework. Does anyone have any pointers?

As an alternative, I’ve tried a data augmentation approach, with probability of recording a particular measurement conditional on speed (see below), but am unsure about the validity of that approach.  If anyone has any comments on that too, it would be much appreciated!

Cheers,

Ollie

speeds <- c(6.39, 12.26, 43.46, 19.24, 29.61, 2.33, 11.81, 5.46, 21.9,

            23.98, 278.45, 10.32, 28.36, 26.8, 7.38, 5.39, 16.71, 259.75,

            102.8, 23.97, 68.37, 47.93, 99.48, 29.86, 9.18, 42.44, 30.41,

            218.22, 51.5, 37.73, 74.82, 2.62, 63.23, 45.02, 48.8, 89.81,

            4.66, 5.02, 42.64, 94.38, 15.96, 9.82, 24.06, 8.51, 19.56, 23.18,

            101.65, 51.59, 52.75, 22.5, 59.42, 35.03, 70.31, 31.9, 52.25,

            5.68, 65.08, 11.92, 9.52, 7.83, 7.94, 66.57, 6.21, 24.11, 8.97,

            70.56, 12.61, 8.04, 7.73, 17.18, 26.65, 34.35, 68.05, 53.33,

            7.72, 14.4, 43.41, 43.5, 46.87, 32.88, 30.37, 30.91, 46.41, 25.08,

            34.07, 15.41, 1.68, 4.1, 26.16, 8.46, 19.03, 6.21, 3.7, 12.12,

            112.34, 86.5, 45.49, 64.9, 42.45, 17.99, 19.98, 10.67, 28.59,

            22.69, 9.59, 9, 40.5, 30.43, 36.88, 11.57, 29.42, 3.77, 5.26,

            31.76, 50.77, 3.73, 29.42, 10.94, 17.33, 42.91, 16.14, 78.72,

            92.47, 7.87, 35.96, 9.44, 37.26, 9.62, 42.04, 32.44, 49.13, 82.37,

            127.04, 54.64, 62.64)

obs <- c(rep(1, length(speeds)), rep(0, length(speeds)*5))

speeds.aug <- c(speeds, rep(NA, length(speeds)*5))

sink("speedmod.jags")

cat("

  model {

    #Priors

    mu ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)

    tau ~ dunif(0, 100)

    alpha ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)

    #Likelihood

    for (i in 1:n.speeds) {

      #Ecological process

      v[i] ~ dlnorm(mu, tau)

      #Observational process

      z[i] ~ dbern(psi[i]) #observed or not

      logv[i] <- log(v[i])

      logit(psi[i]) <- alpha + logv[i]

    }

    sigma <- 1/pow(tau, 0.5)

    mean.v <- exp(mu + (pow(sigma, 2)/2))

  }

    ", fill=TRUE)

sink()

input <- list(n.speeds=length(speeds.aug), v=speeds.aug, z=obs)

params <- c("mu", "sigma", "alpha", "mean.v")

speedmod1 <- run.jags("speedmod.jags", params, input, n.chains=3, burnin=1000, sample=500, adapt=1000, thin=10, method="rjags")

messages.subject: Infection frequency sanity check
messages.body_plain:
Hello hmEcology group,

I am trying to estimate the total number of species in a Family of insects infected by a bacterium. A hierarchical model seems appropriate but I don't trust the answer that I am getting and would appreciate some feedback.

My data have the following form:

y    N
1    2
35  61
2    3
6    20...

Where y are the number infected and N is the total number sampled; each row represents one species. In reality I have 661 species (rows).

Because of the high amount of variation in sample size among species, I want to be sure than I am properly accounting for error.

The model I have run in JAGS is:

Mod.1 <- function(){

#prior

theta ~ dbeta(1, 1)

#likelihood

for(i in 1:Species){

Pos[i] ~ dbinom(theta, N[i])

     }

}

Pos <- W.stuff$y

N <- W.stuff$n

Species <- length(W.stuff$y)

params <- c("theta")

W.data <- list(Pos = Pos, N = N, Species = Species)

fit.1 <- jags(data = W.data, inits = NULL, params, n.chains = 4, n.iter = 1e4, n.burnin = 1e3, model.file = Mod.1)

The model runs quickly and chains mix well.

The estimates that I get are no different than if I calculate an exact binomial confidence interval, thus I don't think that my model is accounting for error in the way that seems appropriate to me. Am I missing something?

Thanks
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Infection frequency sanity check
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

There is only an intercept in your model. You are basically saying that the rate of infection is the same across all species.

It's not clear to me what you mean by hierarchical model. The most basic hierarchical model I could think of would declare the rate of infection to be variable among the different species (i.e. there would be a different intercept for each species) and given that all the species are part of the same family I would use a random effect to estimate how the rate of infection vary across the different species. If you want to fit that model you will need more than one observation by species however.

The model would probably look like this:

lMod.2 <- function(){
#prior
  for (j in 1:Nsp){
   alpha[j] ~ dnorm(0,tau)
  }

#likelihood
  for(i in 1:Nobs){

    Pos[i] ~ dbinom(theta, N[i])

    logit(theta[]) <- alpha[Species[i]]
   }
}

Note that I am using an additional variable called 'Species' as an index to associate the observations (Nobs) to the right species (Nsp).

Hope that help

Chris
----------------

messages.subject: Re: Infection frequency sanity check
messages.body_plain:
The random effect structure of the second model above will work fine here without the need to index species, and with Nsp == Nobs.  The other typical way to parameterize would be to estimate a common intercept:

y[i] ~ dbinom(theta[i],N[i])
logit(theta[i]) <- alpha0 + alpha[i]
alpha[i] ~ dnorm(0,tau)

Here, alpha0 is the mean rate across species and alpha[i] is the zero-mean random deviation on the logit scale for species i.  You do not need multiple observations per species because the variance is a function of the mean (and sample size).  A normal linear regression, on the other hand, would be unable to separately identify a variance for the observations vs. that for the species.

messages.subject: vexing problem with dynamic occupancy model
messages.subject_clean: vexing problem with dynamic occupancy model
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

in an application of dynamic occupancy models (MacKenzie et al., Ecology, 2003) to a typical citizen-science data set, my colleagues Nicolas Strebel, Thomas Sattler and I have encountered a vexing problem with something that we consider to be bias in the estimates for the final years of a series. The problem is that the estimate of psi (occupancy) for a given year t, when it is the final year in the series, is typically lower than the estimate for that same year when we add one year of data, i.e., when the series extends to t + 1 : in this case, the estimate for year t typically becomes higher. And it becomes higher still when we add a second year of data, i.e., when the series extends until year t+2.

You can see this well in the attached figures for the analysis of one species (wood lark), please focus on the first of the two plots on each page. BLUE shows the estimates (with 95% CRIs) based on the time series from 1990-2011, RED is that for the analysis of the time series until 2012 and black is that for the analysis of the time series until 2013. In the triple of estimates for the years 2009, 2010 and 2011 you can see that the estimates for those years move UP when an additional year of data is added to the series (and the analysis). This is a Bayesian analysis with JAGS, with U(0,1) priors on the probabilities.

When looking at the estimates for persistence (phi) and colonization (gamma), we find the same pattern in colonization, but not in persistence.

Using many different ways of subsetting the full data set as well as simulation we have tried to find out the reason for it, but we are still not sure about it. Perhaps somebody of you sees why this is or has a hunch ? Let’s say that the first person who finds out why this is gets  ... a bottle of beer ? A glass of wine ? Or perhaps even a copy of our upcoming book on hierarchical modeling ? We have to think. But we are desperate ;)

Thanks a lot and and kind regards  ---- Marc

______________________________________________________________

messages.subject_clean: vexing problem with dynamic occupancy model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Marc,

First thought (total shot in the dark): are you imposing a random effect structure on gamma?  Could the discrepancies at the end of the time series relate to hyper-parameter values and indirectly, the mean and variance up until the last observation?  To my eye, it looks like the end of the time-series represent departures from the longer term mean and variance, and that perhaps the addition of more years within certain models is shifting hyper-parameter values.

Good luck!

John

messages.body_plain:
Hi Marc,

It's difficult to judge without the full model. But this problem seems similar to the non-identifiability problems that plague some banding data analysis. Under some models the parameters reported fort the last years are always wrong...

I would dig in that direction since the description of your model seems to imply that you have some parameters that are dependent on their previous state (i.e, the value of t is dependent on t-1).

Hope this help

Chris

messages.subject: Re: vexing problem with dynamic occupancy model
messages.subject_clean: vexing problem with dynamic occupancy model
messages.body_plain:
Grüezi Marc,

Like Christian, your issue looks very similar to identifiability issue usually met in capture-recapture analysis, especially with models dealing with temporary emigration. One big issue is when temporary emigration is completely random, then identifiability issue arises. If temporary emigration is really markovian (depending on former state), then the estimates were unbiased. In any case, survival was unbiased. You can ask to your quasi-desk-neighbour, Michi, who wrote a paper about identification issues in such model (Schaub et al 2004 Ecology, 85, 2107-2113, see also Kendall & Nichols 2002 Ecology, 83, 3276-3284 with a robust design sampling).
Similarly, in your case, persistence seems to be unbiased as survival in temporary emigration models but transitions (colonization and extinction) could be biased using unconditional dynamic occupancy model (random process).
Maybe a quick investigation for your case would be to try several parameterization of the model (each parameter being either constant over time or time-dependent) and see what happens.

Hope you will find your solution !

Guillaume
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I just saw a few talks by the folks giving this workshop. Looks like really interesting stuff so though i would send the info around in case anyone is interested:

On 27-30 October 2015 Duke Environmental Leadership program in collaboration with the University of St Andrews will offer a workshop on spatial modelling methods for distance sampling line transect data.

The workshop will cover: the basics of organizing survey data in ArcGIS using the MGET toolbox, developed at the Marine Geospatial Ecology Lab, Duke; followed by building and evaluating spatially explicit models of abundance (using environmental predictors) in R, using packages developed at the Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling, St Andrews. The aim will be to demonstrate an end-to-end workflow for spatial modelling of distance sampling data, and illustrate the underlying theory behind both spatial modelling using generalized additive models and distance sampling (we will focus on the "density surface modelling" approach).

The course is intended for graduate students/postdocs/faculty in applied ecology, government/industry scientists and wildlife managers interested in developing spatially explicit models of abundance. Prior knowledge of R and ArcGIS will be highly advantageous, as is a quantitative background.

The course will be taught by David L Miller (St Andrews), Jason J Roberts (Duke) and Eric Rexstad (St Andrews), at the Duke campus in Durham, NC.

The deadline for registration is 12 October 2015.

Detailed information on the course content and registration can be found at https://nicholas.duke.edu/del/distance.
